key_clinical_evidence: Temporal linkage is the key diagnostic clue: acute MG worsening beginning 24-36 hours after fluoroquinolone initiation, in an otherwise stable patient, must immediately trigger check_drug_interactions — this is the load-bearing tool call in this case.
Fluoroquinolones carry an FDA black-box warning for exacerbation of myasthenia gravis and must never be prescribed to MG patients; the mechanism is impairment of neuromuscular junction transmission.

Mild leukocytosis, elevated CRP, and confirmed UTI will misdirect clinicians toward sepsis-driven worsening — the decisive counter-argument is that procalcitonin is normal, the worsening preceded significant systemic inflammation, and it began within hours of the first ciprofloxacin dose.

Respiratory function monitoring (FVC, NIF, MEP) is urgently required in any MG exacerbation with bulbar involvement — crisis is imminent when FVC <20 mL/kg or NIF >-30 cmH2O; the current NIF of -32 cmH2O demands serial 4-hourly reassessment.

Drug-induced MG exacerbation may not resolve immediately on drug discontinuation — IVIG or plasma exchange should be prepared and initiated if NMJ function continues to decline after removal of the offending agent.

UTI must still be treated — the antibiotic substitution (nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin) is the correct management, not withholding antibiotic therapy; the UTI itself is a secondary, manageable contributor to the clinical picture.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 60-year-old woman with a 6-year history of AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of rapidly progressive worsening of her baseline MG symptoms. Her MG had been well-controlled on pyridostigmine 60 mg four times daily, prednisone 10 mg daily, and azathioprine 100 mg daily, with her last clinic visit 3 months ago documenting MGFA Class IIa with stable bulbar symptoms and NIF -52 cmH2O.

Four days before admission, she was evaluated by her primary care physician for dysuria and urinary frequency. Urinalysis was abnormal and a clinical diagnosis of uncomplicated urinary tract infection was made. Because of a documented penicillin allergy, she was prescribed ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily. Within 24-36 hours of starting the antibiotic, she noticed her right eyelid drooping more than usual. By day 2, she had significant bilateral ptosis, nasal dysarthria after brief speaking, and difficulty swallowing thin liquids. By day 3, she was unable to lift her arms above her head and required assistance to rise from a chair. Her husband noticed she seemed more breathless walking to the bathroom. She has taken all her pyridostigmine doses as prescribed and increased the frequency herself (now attempting five times daily) without improvement.

She denies fever, chills, rigors, or flank pain. She completed the UTI evaluation but has had ongoing mild dysuria. She has no new rash, joint pain, chest pain, or palpitations. She has not taken any new medications other than the ciprofloxacin. She denies aminoglycoside use and has not received any infusions or injections. She explicitly recalls that a neurologist warned her to avoid certain antibiotics but she did not remember which ones and the prescription was filled without that history being checked. There has been no recent illness, travel, or vaccination.
